slides.title: Purpose and indications
bullets: A parasite is an organism that lives, for its whole life or part of its life cycle, at the expense of another organism (the host); parasites can be found in stool, blood, urine, sputum and tissues.
Medically important parasites are divided into protozoa (single-celled; not all pathogenic) and helminths (multicellular worms; always pathogenic).
In stool protozoa appear as trophozoites and cysts, helminths as eggs, larvae, adult worms or their fragments.

slides.title: Purpose and indications
bullets: The test is done to find infections that cause diarrhoea, weight loss and malabsorption, chronic infections with serious complications, to tell amoebic from bacterial dysentery when stool contains blood and mucus, and to follow local infestation (for example pinworm).

slides.title: Collecting and storing the specimen
bullets: A wide-mouthed container with a tight lid is needed — clean, dry, airtight and free of disinfectant residue; paper, cardboard and matchboxes are not suitable.
About 10 mL of liquid stool is taken and examined within 15 minutes (motile parasites); formed stool within 1 hour (Aripova: 2 g; the rural-clinic manual: a teaspoon).

slides.title: Collecting and storing the specimen
bullets: A specimen that is too small, or mixed with urine or dirt, is not accepted: urine destroys amoebic trophozoites and dirt interferes with microscopy.
For parasites shed intermittently (for example G. lamblia) several specimens on alternate days may be needed.
The request form gives the patient’s name, the date and, if possible, the time of collection.

slides.title: Collecting and storing the specimen
bullets: If the specimen cannot be examined at once it may be kept for a few hours in a refrigerator or the coolest place in the laboratory, but it is analysed the same day; protect it from sun and heat.

slides.title: Macroscopic examination
bullets: 1. Check that the label details match the request form; open specimens one at a time.
2. Note colour, consistency and the presence of blood, mucus, pus, worms, tapeworm segments or adult pinworms.
3. Close the container; move to the next specimen or prepare the wet mount at once.

slides.title: Macroscopic examination
bullets: 4. When many specimens arrive, examine those with blood and mucus first (for dysentery amoeba), then watery stool — motile trophozoites are found there.
5. Record the results; normal stool is formed, dark brown, and free of blood, mucus, pus and worms.

slides.title: Wet mount from watery stool (with eosin)
bullets: 1. Number the specimen and the slide with the same number.

2. With an applicator take a little stool containing particles of blood and pus and put it near one edge of the slide; cover with a cover glass without saline and press gently through a wipe to make it thin.
3. Put a drop of eosin at the other end — do this before stool touches the slide, so the dropper is not contaminated.

slides.title: Wet mount from watery stool (with eosin)
bullets: 4. Mix a little more stool with the eosin and lower the cover glass, held by a corner, without air bubbles.
5. Examine at once: if the slide dries, trophozoites and flagellates lose their motility.
6. Eosin does not stain living trophozoites — it gives a pink background that makes them easier to see.

slides.title: Wet mount from formed stool (saline and iodine)
bullets: 1. Number the specimen and the slide; put a drop of 0.85% saline on one half of the slide and a drop of 2% iodine on the other, before any stool touches it.
2. Mix the stool with an applicator so that any parasites are spread evenly.
3. Mix a match-head-sized piece first with saline, then another piece of the same specimen with iodine.

slides.title: Wet mount from formed stool (saline and iodine)
bullets: 4. Make a thin, even smear: printed text should be readable through it; a smear that is too thick or too thin makes diagnosis difficult.
5. Cover each with a cover glass without air bubbles and examine at once, before they dry.

slides.title: Microscopy
bullets: 1. View the slide with the 10× objective and the condenser sufficiently closed (too much light lowers contrast); examine the whole slide systematically, moving it forward and back or up and down.
2. Look for motile trophozoites, flagellates, helminth eggs, larvae and cysts.
3. To identify colourless parasites set the condenser for more contrast and change to the 40× objective.

slides.title: Microscopy
bullets: 4. Before reporting “no parasites found” examine several fields with the 40× objective.
5. In the iodine slide cysts are identified by size, shape, nuclei and number of inclusions.
6. Record and count all parasites found in the saline slide.

slides.title: Protozoa: key features
rows: Entamoeba histolytica
Moves in one direction; one nucleus with a central karyosome; ingested red cells inside — a diagnostic sign
Round, 1–4 nuclei (in the iodine slide), central karyosome
Giardia lamblia
Pear-shaped, spins quickly; sucking disc on the ventral side, two nuclei, four pairs of flagella
Small oval, four nuclei (sometimes hard to see), axostyles, remnants of flagella

slides.title: Protozoa: key features
rows: Balantidium coli
Large oval, rotating movement, cilia, macronucleus; often red cells inside
Large round, thick-walled, nucleus well stained by iodine, contractile vacuoles
Isospora belli
Oval cyst (oocyst), usually with a granular zygote; iodine does not stain it (in an unstained wet mount)

slides.title: Notes on telling protozoa apart
bullets: Cysts of E. histolytica are told from cysts of non-pathogenic amoebae (E. hartmanni, E. coli, E. buetschlii, E. nana) by size, number of nuclei, and the presence of peripheral chromatin and a glycogen vacuole.

Trophozoites of non-pathogenic flagellates (Chilomastix mesnili, Trichomonas hominis, Enteromonas hominis, Retortamonas intestinalis) have one nucleus and fewer flagella; their cysts are smaller and lack flagellar remnants — this separates them from Giardia.

Cryptosporidium parvum and Cyclospora cayetanensis may be seen in a wet mount but are easier to find with the modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain; if they are suspected the patient is referred to a large laboratory.

slides.title: Notes on telling protozoa apart
bullets: Not all protozoa are pathogenic, so correct identification of each prevents a wrong diagnosis.

slides.title: Tapeworms (cestodes)
rows: Taenia saginata, T. solium
The eggs cannot be told apart: round-oval, thick brown radially striated shell, an embryo with 3 pairs of hooks inside. Eggs are shed irregularly, so the diagnosis is often made from segments
Hymenolepis nana
Egg oval or round, colourless or pale grey; embryo with 3 pairs of hooks, thread-like polar filaments at each end
Hymenolepis diminuta
Egg round, yellow, thick-shelled; 3 pairs of hooks, no polar filaments

slides.title: Tapeworms (cestodes)
rows: Diphyllobothrium latum
Egg yellow-brown, oval; a granular mass of yolk cells around the embryo, a lid at one end (hard to see)
Dipylidium caninum
Segments look like pumpkin seeds and are motile in the specimen; eggs lie in capsules (8–15 each)

slides.title: Roundworms (nematodes)
rows: Ascaris lumbricoides
Fertilised egg round or oval, yellow, covered by a thick rough albuminous coat, granular mass in the centre
Enterobius vermicularis
Egg smooth, shell colourless, oval with one side flattened, larva inside; eggs are usually found in a perianal specimen
Trichuris trichiura
Barrel-shaped egg, a colourless plug at each pole, smooth double shell, yellow-brown, granular mass in the centre

slides.title: Roundworms (nematodes)
rows: Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus
Egg oval, colourless, thin-shelled, looks divided into 4–8 cells; in stool kept longer than 12 hours a larva is visible, after 24 hours it may hatch (tell it from a Strongyloides larva)
Strongyloides stercoralis
Mainly motile larvae in stool, eggs rarely

slides.title: Flukes (trematodes)
rows: Clonorchis (Opisthorchis) sinensis, O. felineus, O. viverrini

Very small yellow-brown eggs shaped like a light bulb, smooth shell, a clear lid at the narrowed end. Hard to find in a direct wet mount — if suspected the material is concentrated by the formalin-ether method (large laboratory)

slides.title: Flukes (trematodes)
rows: Schistosoma species

Large yellow-brown eggs; the species is told by the position of the spine: S. mansoni — lateral, S. intercalatum — terminal, S. japonicum — a small lateral knob. Intestinal schistosomiasis occurs with blood and mucus in the stool
Fasciola hepatica, F. gigantica
Large oval yellow-brown eggs, smooth shell, lid indistinct

slides.title: Concentration methods (large laboratories)
rows: Formalin-ether
Small eggs: Opisthorchis/Clonorchis, Taenia
Needs highly flammable ether or ethyl acetate; not recommended for small laboratories
Flotation in saturated sodium chloride
Eggs of Ascaris and hookworms
Cheap; usually not recommended for the eggs of other parasites
Flotation in zinc sulfate
Cysts of G. lamblia, E. histolytica; eggs of Trichuris, Opisthorchis
Zinc sulfate does not kill the parasites — take care

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Non-parasitic structures may be mistaken for parasites: vegetable and muscle fibres, pollen, starch cells, fat particles, yeasts, spores, soaps, hairs, fatty-acid crystals and air bubbles.
Laxatives, antacids, contrast media and some antibiotics may interfere with finding parasites.
If the slide dries or the specimen is late, motile trophozoites are not found; a parasite shed intermittently may be missed in a single specimen.
With too much light colourless eggs cannot be seen — close the condenser.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Quality depends on standardised methods and the skill of the staff: the laboratory should have positive slides or pictures against which the parasites found are compared.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Stool specimens may contain parasites, bacteria and viruses — take the usual precautions.
Wear single-use gloves; wash the hands after work.
In concentration work zinc sulfate does not kill parasites; ether and ethyl acetate are highly flammable — work away from open flame.
Disinfect used containers, slides and instruments (according to the regulation).

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/4
bullets: Specimen: Stool (2–3 samples a few days apart; in preservative vials when needed)

What it is used for: The test shows whether intestinal parasites are causing symptoms of a gut infection and whether treatment is working. Such symptoms include diarrhea lasting a few days, belly pain, blood or mucus in stool, foul greasy floating stools, nausea, gas, fever and weight loss. It is more likely to be ordered with serious symptoms (dehydration), a weakened immune system, or possible exposure (untreated water, travel, contact with an infected person).

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/4
bullets: Physiology: Intestinal parasites live and reproduce in the digestive system; they and their eggs are passed in stool. Invisible traces of contaminated stool reach water, soil, food and surfaces, and infection follows when they are swallowed. Some worms, such as hookworms, enter through the skin, especially when walking barefoot.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 3/4
bullets: A wet mount shows protozoan trophozoites, cysts and oocysts as well as helminth eggs and larvae: a small amount of stool is placed on a slide and, if fairly solid, mixed with a drop or two of saline; ideally two smears are made on one slide, one stained with iodine. The whole coverslip is scanned systematically with the 10× objective. Permanent stained slides identify trophozoites and cysts to species — at least 200–300 oil-immersion fields are examined. Size is a key feature, so the microscope is calibrated with an ocular micrometer.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 4/4
bullets: Direct (wet) microscopy is done in two drops: saline (warmed to 37 °C) shows motile trophozoites, Lugol’s iodine (iodine–acetic acid) shows cyst nuclei clearly — iodine immobilises trophozoites. Use liquid or mucoid stool for trophozoites and formed stool for eggs.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result
cols: A positive result means parasites and/or eggs were found — there are intestinal parasites. The report also gives the type and how many were seen. Treatment depends on the parasite and general health; plenty of fluids help prevent dehydration from diarrhea and vomiting.

A negative result means no parasites or eggs were found: either there are none, or too few were in the sample. Parasites are not shed in stool every day, so collection is repeated after a negative first exam — CDC advises examining three specimens passed 2–3 days apart when possible.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/9
bullets: Pre-analytics: Collect stool in a dry, clean, leak-proof container with no urine, water or soil. Fresh stool is examined, processed or preserved immediately; an unpreserved specimen kept only under refrigeration is suitable for antigen testing only. Without a kit, the specimen is split between 10% formalin and PVA (polyvinyl alcohol): one volume of stool to three volumes of preservative, mixed well, with formed stool broken up.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/9
bullets: Collect stool in a clean, dry, lidded container without preservative; no urine (not from a bedpan), and include any worms or segments passed. WHO advises examining it within 1–4 hours and, if several arrive together, looking first at liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stools — motile amoebae die quickly. Lyubina (1984) and Aripova (2007) also reject matchboxes or paper.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/9
bullets: For shipping to a distant laboratory a preservative is added: 10% formalin (for wet mounts and sedimentation), PVA (for permanent stains such as trichrome), MIF or SAF/TIF mixtures. Dadayev (2004) also notes that stool for amoebiasis must be preserved (or delivered quickly).

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/9
bullets: Interferences: Certain drugs and compounds make stool unsatisfactory for examination: antacids, kaolin, mineral oil and other oily materials, non-absorbable antidiarrheals, barium or bismuth (7–10 days to clear), antimicrobial agents (2–3 weeks) and gallbladder dyes (3 weeks). Collect before they are given or wait until their effects have passed.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/9
bullets: Limitations: Each preservative has drawbacks: formalin preserves helminth eggs, larvae and cysts well but not trophozoite morphology, and long fixation can interfere with PCR; PVA preserves trophozoites and cysts well but not helminth eggs or larvae, and is unsuitable for concentration procedures. Using both is therefore recommended. If PCR is needed, the specimen is collected to its specific requirements.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 6/9
bullets: For pinworm, a stool test is usually not useful — stool rarely contains enough eggs; the perianal tape test is used instead.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 7/9
bullets: Concentration is needed when parasites are few. In flotation (e.g., Willis saturated NaCl; zinc sulfate) eggs rise in a dense solution: good for hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia and Trichuris eggs, but not for fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae or protozoa — some eggs do not float and cyst and egg walls may collapse. Sedimentation (formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate) recovers more species, is easier, and CDC recommends it for general laboratories; ethyl acetate is less flammable than ether.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 8/9
bullets: In the Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear about 0.5 g of sieved stool is cleared under glycerol-soaked cellophane (with malachite green or methylene blue); it detects and counts helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma, and slides can be stored and shipped. It is unsuitable for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis and protozoa.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 9/9
bullets: No single method finds every parasite: always do direct microscopy before concentration (motile forms are not seen in concentrated preparations). If the result is negative, the doctor may request repeat samples on other days.

slides.title: Saline wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Motile trophozoites, moderate numbers of eggs and cysts, red cells, fat
Limitations: May miss scanty parasites; use liquid stool and saline warmed to 37 °C for trophozoites

slides.title: Iodine (Lugol) mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Cyst nuclei and glycogen vacuoles; telling Giardia and amoeba cysts apart
Limitations: Trophozoites stop moving — check motility in saline

slides.title: Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma; egg counts; slides can be stored and shipped
Limitations: Not for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis or protozoa

slides.title: Flotation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Light eggs rise in a dense solution (saturated NaCl — Willis; zinc sulfate): hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia, Trichuris
Limitations: Fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae, protozoa; cyst and egg walls may collapse

slides.title: Sedimentation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate: most eggs, larvae and cysts; CDC recommends it for general laboratories
Limitations: Motile forms are not seen — do a wet mount first; ether is flammable, ethyl acetate is safer

slides.title: Preservatives (shipping)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool · 1/2
bullets: 10% formalin — for wet mounts and sedimentation; preserves eggs and cysts well, trophozoites less so.
PVA — for permanent (trichrome) stains; MIF, SAF or TIF — mixtures for wet mounts.

slides.title: Preservatives (shipping)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool · 2/2
bullets: Fresh stool without preservative is examined within 1–4 hours; liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stool first.

slides.title: Pinworm: adhesive tape
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: Pinworm eggs are scarce in stool — collect them with tape from the perianal skin.
In the morning before washing or using the toilet; repeat on three consecutive days.
